overview.headline: How Congress turns bills into laws and House Senate roles differ

keyPoints.point: Congress serves as the federal lawmaking branch that creates new laws
keyPoints.quote: Congress is the lawmaking branch of the federal government.

keyPoints.point: An introduced bill goes to a committee to research discuss and make changes before voting
keyPoints.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.

keyPoints.point: The president can approve and sign a bill into law or refuse approval through a veto
keyPoints.quote: The president can approve the bill and sign it into law. Or the president can refuse to approve a bill. This is called a veto.

keyPoints.point: House and Senate differ on tax legislation nominations treaties and voting procedures
keyPoints.quote: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation

keyTerms.gloss: proposal for a new law or change to an existing law
keyTerms.quote: A bill is a proposal for a new law or a change to an existing law.

keyTerms.gloss: group whose members will research and discuss a bill
keyTerms.quote: Once a bill is introduced, it is assigned to a committee whose members will research, discuss, and make changes to the bill.

keyTerms.gloss: president refusal to approve a bill when called to consider it
keyTerms.quote: Or the president can refuse to approve a bill. This is called a veto.

keyTerms.gloss: action where a bill cannot be overridden by Congress after session ends
keyTerms.quote: This action is called a pocket veto, and it cannot be overridden by Congress.

keyTerms.gloss: tax and revenue-related measure initiated by the House
keyTerms.quote: Only the House can initiate tax and revenue-related legislation
